components.gap: The inferential interpretation is reconstructed only as far as the Section 2 premises (J1)-(J5) and the application limits. The paper's own stated justificatory claims are missing, so the interpretation is not shown to be conditional on all the premises the paper states. Missing claims: (i) the rules of statistical mechanics are justified as inference independently of physical argument and of experimental verification, and the maximum-entropy estimates remain the best obtainable from the information whatever experiment shows, even as predictions become indefinite (abstract p. 620; p. 626); (ii) the inferential reading makes the hypotheses of ergodicity, metric transitivity and equal a priori probabilities unnecessary. The paper argues this from three points: the laws of motion add no information beyond measurement for equilibrium prediction; there is no rational basis for excluding any state the information allows, which acts like an ergodic hypothesis whether or not the system is ergodic; and the conclusion section reaches the usual relations without ensembles or ergodic arguments (abstract; Sec. 1 p. 621 'reversal' of the usual reasoning; p. 623; pp. 624-625 including the uniform-integrals argument; p. 627; Sec. 6 p. 629); (iii) inventing a fictitious ensemble cannot change the subjective standing of the probabilities (p. 626). None of these appears at 043 lines 398-532 or elsewhere on the route: ergodicity, metric transitivity, equal a priori probabilities and ensemble-based justification are never mentioned in 043/044. 043 lines 704-709 nonetheless present Sections 1-6 as the treated extent. The required extent fixes 'the complete ... inferential argument in the original paper', so the reconstruction is not complete.

defect_observations.observation: Parts of the paper's maximum-entropy construction are not supplied anywhere on the route. Missing: Jaynes's (2-15), the maximum-entropy estimates of derivatives of the constraint functions with respect to external parameters (p. 623), on which the forces (3-4) rest (p. 624). Lines 483-484 say the usual relations (3-1)-(3-4) are 'recovered' without it. Also missing: Sec. 5's general variation result (5-1)-(5-3) (variation of lambda_0 = ln Z and of the maximal entropy; multipliers as integrating factors, i.e. quantities 'statistically conjugate' to f_k; p. 627); (5-4)-(5-8), where the multiplier equals the derivative of the maximal entropy with respect to the declared mean, lambda = 1/T; and the point that the information may be supplied as the conjugate multiplier instead of the expectation (p. 628). Lines 514-517 reduce all of this to a one-line rigor caveat. These belong to 'the complete maximum-entropy construction' fixed by the unit's required extent. No component description clearly owns them; C03 explains multipliers fully as dual variables but never gives their sensitivity or conjugate reading. Recorded for the user's decision, not scored as a C03 failure.
The p. 630 conclusion is reported without the reason the paper gives for it, namely that the method guarantees no unconscious arbitrary assumptions have been introduced. Part of the C04 gap.

The asymmetry of Jaynes's regression lines is tied to the changed-constraint example. Jaynes's own explanation (p. 626) is not cited: the asymmetry arises because the possible values were specified in the coordinate x rather than g, which is the reference-measure point that 044 develops. This is missed source grounding, not a coverage gap.

The factory example is credited to Hajek and Staffel, here and in the Sources paragraph at lines 262-264; rationality-4-1.tex lines 347-354 also call it 'their factory example'. The source (p. 244) presents it as van Fraassen's (1989) illustration. rationality-4-1.tex names van Fraassen only among the authors the source points to. This is an attribution nuance.

Two minor empirical or historical remarks in the source are neither presented nor classified: the uncited statement that Brier scores are used to score weather forecasters and political analysts (p. 242), and the statement that the literature on the Principal Principle has overlooked Lewis's change of formulation (p. 243, with note 7). They are not judged component-failing because they are asides, not examples or argument steps.

The source attributes the claim that the accuracy argument needs one specific strictly proper score to Bronfman's unpublished manuscript (p. 242). Neither the dependent-source table nor rationality-4-1.tex lines 213-222 names that manuscript. The table says it lists every theorem and finding reported as established elsewhere. This is a claim about the structure of an argument rather than a theorem or finding, so it is not scored as a C05 failure, but a reviewer may want the dependency recorded.
